name: Beagle 2 lander
headline: Lost on Christmas Day 2003, spotted 11 years later by a NASA orbiter, partly unfolded
story: On Christmas Day 2003, Beagle 2 was due to fall through the Martian sky onto Isidis Planitia, slowed by a heat shield, parachutes and airbags. Six days earlier, ESA's Mars Express had released it toward the planet. The small British-led lander, named after Darwin's ship, carried a miniature laboratory to look for signs of life. It never called home.

Attempts to contact it went on through January and February 2004. On 6 February, the Beagle 2 Management Board declared it lost, and for more than a decade no one knew what had happened. Then Michael Croon, a former member of the Mars Express operations team, spotted it in images from HiRISE, the camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

The find was announced on 16 January 2015. Beagle 2 had landed about 5 kilometers from the center of its target, with its rear cover and parachute nearby. Its solar panels had only partly unfolded, most likely leaving its radio antenna covered. It still rests there, half open, on the plains of Isidis.

images.caption: 15 December 2014: the bright speck on the plain is Beagle 2, seen from orbit by HiRISE. The scale bar is 10 meters.
June 2014: the lander, its rear cover and what is probably its parachute, scattered a short distance apart on Isidis Planitia.
Two HiRISE views from 2013 and 2014, with the Sun at different angles, catch glints in different places on the lander: a sign that more than one panel opened.
